doc.title: Plas Johnson interviewed by Monk Rowe, Sarasota, Florida, April 12, 1996

title: The Rod Stewart solo and multi-track editing
summary: Plas may not be the soloist on the Rod Stewart record, since producers call several saxophonists and splice solos together.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: I have had students that just had to play that you know. They really want to get that sax lick down the way you did it. It’s kind of hard. Tell me about the Rod Stewart thing, how that came about.

I was just called. I’ve read recently that with the advent of multi-track, producers many times would call several soloists to play the same solo. And so I found out recently that that may not be my solo on Rod Stewart’s record.

A saxophonist by the name of Jerry Jumonville also was called in and Jerry is not a student of mine but he’s been a fan of mine for years, and we talk about pieces and he likes my style, and so actually when I heard the solo I really thought it was me, but I don’t think so because I’ve seen on Jerry’s record he put that he played it so it just might be his solo.
Well if it’s not you it’s somebody trying to be you.
Well exactly. But I was called and I did play. So who knows what comes out of it? And that happens many times.
Or sometimes it could be half you—

Well that’s another thing that happens where you play a twelve-bar solo and you might have four bars from track seven and the last two bars from track fifteen and somewhere in the middle from another track. And it can be done electronically so that it sounds like one solo. In fact I’ve had it done to my own solos. And I liked it.
I guess if the producer has got good taste and good ears you know.
